sm: The Supreme Court is hearing argument in a challenge by Ken Jouppi, an eighty-three-year-old Alaska bush pilot, to the forfeiture of his ninety-five thousand dollar airplane. In April 2012, state troopers with a warrant searched his plane before a flight from Fairbanks to Beaver, a dry village of about forty-eight people with no road access, and found the equivalent of three cases of beer belonging to a passenger. The passenger pleaded guilty, while Jouppi was convicted at trial, sentenced to three days in prison and fined fifteen hundred dollars, and prosecutors also sought his plane. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the forfeiture as not grossly disproportional. Jouppi argues the Excessive Fines Clause requires looking at his own culpability, citing the 1998 Bajakajian decision, and he says the case is really about one six-pack.

Jouppi argues the Alaska court judged his wrongdoing at an abstract level, and says that approach would justify forfeiting a car for a seatbelt violation or minor speeding. He also criticizes the state court for comparing the plane's value to the maximum fine for any class A misdemeanor, a category covering very different offenses. Alaska replies that he loaded two cases and four six-packs of beer, about nine gallons, bound for an isolated village hurt by alcohol. It says state law requires forfeiture when a pilot knowingly brings alcohol into a dry community, to keep the plane from being reused and to deter others. The state adds that the Alaska court looked at his actual circumstances, and that forfeiting ships has a long history in federal law, including in Alaska's territorial days.

The state distinguishes forfeiture of ships and planes used in crimes from forfeiture of currency as in Bajakajian, saying the inquiry for such instrumentalities is whether the property was tainted by unlawful use. Friend-of-the-court briefs split. Fair and Just Prosecution says fines and forfeitures now work as revenue tools, and the Pacific Legal Foundation says property confiscation should turn on individual culpability. The Alaska Legislative Council calls the law a calibrated response to a crisis of rural isolation and says punishment is mainly for legislatures to decide. Former Attorney General William Barr and three former Alaska attorneys general argue that Jouppi's rule would understate the gravity of offenses in the communities where deterrence matters most.
